q: Afraid of looking mean, most tables skip past the cheapest bottle on the page, and trade lore holds that one slot quietly outsells everything around it. Which slot?
accept: second cheapest bottle on the list
second cheapest wine on the list
second cheapest bottle on the page
second cheapest wine on the page
ans: The second-cheapest bottle on the list
exp: Nobody wants to read as the table's economist, so the finger settles one line up from the bottom. Buyers know it, which is why that slot so often carries the list's friendliest margin rather than its finest wine.

q: High on the first page sits a bottle priced beyond what almost anyone will pay, and the buyer never expected it to sell. What is it there to do?
accept: makes the rest of the list look reasonable
making the rest of the list look reasonable
makes the other bottles look reasonable
makes the rest of the list look cheaper
makes the other wines look cheap
make the other wines look cheap
makes the other bottles look cheaper
ans: Anchoring: it makes the rest of the list look reasonable
exp: Its work is done unsold: beside a 900 bottle, 120 reads as restraint. Placement does the arithmetic on the guest's behalf, and the effect costs the venue nothing so long as the bottle finds one buyer a year.

q: Reading down a page priced 40, 48, 58 and 70, a guest can climb toward better wine in small, painless steps. Which pricing tactic built the page?
exp: Each rung asks a little more than the last and never a leap, so the climb from 40 to 70 happens one easy step at a time. Gaps work the other way: a page that jumps from 50 to 95 loses every guest standing at the edge of the jump.

q: Every night a wine bar tips away two open bottles at an average cost of 20, and a 3,000 gas preservation system is proposed. What does the arithmetic say?
opts: Two bottles a night is too small a loss to justify any capital spend
Payback only arrives if glass prices rise alongside the equipment
Gas refills will cost more over a year than the wine they save, so the case fails
About 280 of wine a week stops going down the sink, and 3,000 is eleven weeks of that
exp: Two bottles at 20 is 40 a night and 280 a week, poured away. Against that, 3,000 of kit is under eleven weeks of losses, so the system pays for itself inside three months and everything after that is margin. Preservation is bought with wine that was already being thrown out.

q: Priced to recover its whole cost in one pour, a rare glass finds no takers; priced where guests bite, recovery takes three pours. What settles the argument for the lower price?
opts: An unsold rare bottle can always go back to the distributor for credit, so the downside was never real
Under gas the remainder keeps for weeks, so the bottle can earn its cost back slowly
The lower price still clears the cost, and nothing else about a glass matters
Three pours from a single bottle is the ceiling most licences allow, so the arithmetic can never get worse
exp: Preservation changes the deadline, and the deadline was the whole argument for aggressive pricing. Once the remainder keeps, the bottle can earn its cost across a week of single pours, and the lower price recruits the guests who make that happen.

q: Sunday night closes with the week's unsold open bottles poured down the sink and their cost value entered in the books. Under which heading does that loss go?
exp: Wastage is the counted, explained loss: wine that tired before it sold, priced at cost and written down. Keeping it as its own line matters, because it is the one component of pour cost a manager can actually attack with equipment and discipline.

q: Short and quick-selling is the only safe shape for a by-the-glass page poured without any preservation. What is the page's length being matched to?
accept: speed at which the wines sell
exp: An unprotected open bottle has two or three days of honest life, so the page is sized to what will empty inside that window. Add gas and the constraint relaxes, which is why the length of a by-the-glass page is a statement about the bar's equipment.

q: Through the needle of a preservation device, a 400 bottle gives ten 75 ml tastes. To hold a 25 percent cost on the pour, what must one taste sell for?
exp: Ten tastes from one bottle puts 40 of cost into each; 40 over 0.25 is 160. The arithmetic is the same as any pour cost, only the pour is smaller and the bottle dearer, which is how a 400 wine meets a guest who would never buy it whole.

q: Six bottles a year of a cult Pinot arrive only because the distributor chooses the venue, and the buyer knows the price of staying chosen. What is the venue expected to do in return?
accept: buy the rest of the book
ans: Buy the rest of the book
exp: Scarce wine is currency, and the distributor spends it on accounts that carry the everyday bottles as well. Let those go and the cult ones quietly stop arriving; another venue is always happy to take the whole book.

q: On the owner's nod, two bottles go free of charge to a critic's table. How does a clean set of books record them?
opts: At cost, on a promotion line rather than in beverage cost
As breakage, since the stock left the cellar without any matching sale
At full list price, rung through the till as a sale and immediately voided by a manager
Nowhere, because accounts exist to record transactions and no money changed hands
exp: The bottles are a real cost and a deliberate one, so they move at cost value out of beverage cost and into promotion, where the spend was actually made. Left in beverage cost they poison the percentage; recorded nowhere, the stock count comes up short with nothing to say why.

q: Fourteen bottles left the cellar by the physical count, while the till shows twelve sold and one recorded comp. What does the fourteenth bottle become in the stock report?
exp: Twelve sold and one comped explains thirteen; the fourteenth is variance, the gap between what left and what was accounted for. A steady trickle of it is over-pouring or sloppy recording, a widening one is theft, and neither shows without the count.

q: State law obliges any wine using a Napa sub-appellation such as Oakville or Rutherford to print Napa Valley on the same label. What is that requirement called?
opts: Conjunctive labeling
Nested appellation disclosure
Compound origin marking
Appellation transfer
exp: Nothing federal demands it: the TTB approves an AVA boundary and then says nothing about how the name is used alongside a larger one. California legislated it to stop the parent name being diluted by sub-appellations trading on their own, and Sonoma County growers later won the same protection for theirs.

q: A back label reads Produced and Bottled by, followed by a winery name and its town. How much of the wine must that winery have fermented itself?
opts: Fifty-one percent of it
Eighty-five percent of it
Seventy-five percent of it
All of it
exp: Produced and Made are the two phrases that carry a fermentation threshold, and the federal rule sets both at 75 percent fermented at the stated address. Cellared and Bottled by, Vinted and Bottled by or Prepared and Bottled by cover wine bought in finished and merely given cellar treatment there, and Blended and Bottled by means only that wines of the same class and type were mixed at that address. None of those four tells the guest who actually made it.

q: Eighty percent of a blend comes off Rutherford and the remaining fifth off Oakville, so neither sub-appellation may go on the label. What is the tightest appellation this wine may still claim?
exp: An AVA name needs 85 percent of the fruit from inside its boundary, and no single sub-appellation clears that here. Both benches sit wholly inside Napa Valley, however, so the parent AVA is satisfied at 100 percent and is the tightest claim left. Dropping to Napa County or to California would be legal but needlessly vague.

q: Federal rules would happily let a wine calling itself Sonoma County carry a quarter of its fruit from outside the state altogether. A California statute shuts that door. What does the state demand instead?
accept: all of the fruit must be grown in california
every grape must be grown in california
all the grapes must come from california
all the grapes must be grown in california
all of the grapes must be grown in california
the grapes must all be grown in california
every grape must come from california
all the fruit must come from california
all the fruit has to come from california
100% of the grapes must be grown in california
100% of the fruit must be grown in california
100% of the grapes must be from california
100 percent of the grapes must be grown in california
one hundred percent of the fruit from california
one hundred percent of the grapes from california
every grape has to be grown in california
all of the fruit has to be grown in california
the wine must be entirely from california grapes
exp: Federal law asks only 75 percent for a county or state name, which would let a Sonoma County bottling be topped up from anywhere. California overrides that: a wine carrying any Californian appellation of origin must be made entirely from Californian fruit. It is one of several places where state law is stricter than the federal floor rather than merely different from it.

q: Fruit grown in one state is blended in a cellar with fruit from another, leaving the broadest appellation on the books as the only one available. What may the label no longer state?
accept: the year the grapes were harvested
the year the grapes were picked
exp: Two or three states that are contiguous can share an appellation of their own, with the percentage from each printed on the label, and a wine carrying it keeps its vintage. Where that is not available the wine falls back to American, which is a country-level appellation, and a vintage date is permitted only when the appellation is something other than a country. So the harvest year is the price of the fallback. It is a useful reminder that the appellation on an American label controls far more than geography.
